scope.flow: AtomWallet UserOperation signature validation and relayer submission of a signed UserOperation with a 77-byte signature containing an unsigned validUntil||validAfter suffix
scope.environment: AtomWallet smart contract account (ERC-4337 style UserOperation validation)
evidence: there is an Unauthenticated validUntil and validAfter suffix lets the relayers bypass the AtomWallet’s time-window checks

The bug here in the contract is the `AtomWallet` treats the trailing 12-byte `validUntil || validAfter` suffix in a 77-byte signature as trusted authorization metadata even though those 12 bytes are not authenticated by the signer. During `_validateSignature`, the contract first extracts `validUntil`, `validAfter`, and the stripped 65-byte raw signature from `userOp.signature`, then recovers the signer using only that 65-byte signature, and finally returns validation data containing the extracted timestamps. Because the recovered signer check does not cover the trailing 12 bytes, any relayer or observer holding a valid signed UserOperation can strip the suffix entirely to make the operation

effectively timeless, or rewrite the suffix to make the operation valid earlier or keep it valid longer, without invalidating the signature. As a result, time-limited approvals in `AtomWallet` are not enforceable, and signed wallet actions such as arbitrary calls, token approvals, transfers, or deposit withdrawals can be executed outside the time window the owner intended here where this is came from :
the root of the bug is the `AtomWallet` verifies only the first 65 bytes of a 77-byte signature, while enforcing `validUntil` and `validAfter` from the unsigned trailing 12 bytes.

this bug make any owner who relies on AtomWallet’s 77-byte signature format to authorize a user operation only during a specific time window has no real protection, because a relayer, bundler, or anyone who sees the signature can remove or rewrite the unsigned 12-byte suffix and submit the same operation earlier than intended, after it was supposed to expire, or with a much longer validity period, which breaks time-based authorization guarantees and turns temporary approvals into effectively reusable or indefinitely valid approvals.
